policy_summary: The Non-Compete Clause Rule, issued by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), prohibits employers from entering into non-compete clauses with workers after the rule's effective date. Existing non-compete clauses are unenforceable for most workers, except senior executives, who are exempt from this provision. Employers must notify affected workers about the unenforceability of existing non-competes, and the rule provides model language for this purpose. The rule aims to address the negative effects of non-compete clauses on competition, wages, and labor mobility, while providing clarity on definitions and exceptions.
key_changes: The final rule bans new non-compete clauses for all workers after the effective date (Final Rule, Summary).
Existing non-compete clauses are unenforceable for workers other than senior executives, who are exempt from this provision (Final Rule, Summary).
Employers are required to notify workers with existing non-competes that these clauses are no longer enforceable, using model language provided in the rule (Final Rule, Summary).
The definition of 'employment' was clarified to include work for a person, regardless of classification under other laws (Final Rule, Section III.B).

affected_stakeholders.description: Workers will no longer be bound by non-compete clauses, improving their ability to change jobs and negotiate better wages.
affected_stakeholders.evidence_excerpt: Existing non-competes with workers other than senior executives are not enforceable after the effective date (Final Rule, Summary).

affected_stakeholders.description: Senior executives are exempt from the unenforceability provision for existing non-compete clauses, allowing these agreements to remain in force.
affected_stakeholders.evidence_excerpt: Existing non-competes with senior executives can remain in force; the final rule does not cover such agreements (Final Rule, Summary).

affected_stakeholders.description: Employers must cease entering into new non-compete clauses and notify workers with existing non-competes about their unenforceability.
affected_stakeholders.evidence_excerpt: Employers must provide such workers with existing non-competes notice that they are no longer enforceable (Final Rule, Summary).

affected_stakeholders.description: The rule applies to nonprofits only if they are profit-making enterprises, as determined by a two-part test.
affected_stakeholders.evidence_excerpt: Congress took pains in drafting § 4 to authorize the Commission to regulate so-called nonprofit corporations, associations and all other entities if they are in fact profit-making enterprises (Final Rule, Section III.B).

important_definitions.definition: A partnership, corporation, association, limited liability company, or other legal entity, or a division or subsidiary thereof.
Work for a person, regardless of whether an employment relationship exists under other laws.

findings.claim: Non-compete clauses reduce workers' earnings and labor mobility.

evidence.excerpt: Non-compete clauses negatively affect competition in labor markets, thereby inhibiting optimal matches from being made between employers and workers across the labor force (Proposed Rule, Section I.b).
A nationwide ban on non-compete clauses would increase average earnings by 3.3-13.9% (Proposed Rule, Section I.b).

findings.claim: Non-compete clauses are coercive and exploitative for most workers.

evidence.excerpt: Non-compete clauses force a worker to either stay in a job they want to leave or choose an alternative that likely impacts their livelihood (Proposed Rule, Section I.c).

findings.claim: Employers have alternatives to non-compete clauses for protecting investments.

evidence.excerpt: Employers have alternatives for protecting valuable investments that are much more narrowly tailored to limit impacts on competitive conditions (Proposed Rule, Section I.2).

uncertainty_or_limitations: The causal relationship between non-compete clauses and reduced earnings for workers not subject to these clauses remains partially uncertain due to limitations in available data (Proposed Rule, Section I.c).
The practical impacts of exempting senior executives from the unenforceability provision for existing non-competes are not fully addressed (Final Rule, Summary).
The rule's applicability to nonprofit organizations with complex financial structures may require further clarification (Final Rule, Section III.B).
